articles.title_orig: 'GTA 6' release live updates: Reviews, memes and more as gamers explore and react to Leonida after 13 long years
articles.title_zh: 'GTA 6' release live updates: Reviews, memes and more as gamers explore and react to Leonida after 13 long years
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI is here at last, and gamers around the world can finally play after it launched Thursday. So far, the game, which takes up a whopping 212GB on your PlayStation5 or Xbox , is receiving rave reviews . GTA 6 is streaming all over Twitch, and the memes, clips and hot takes have been pouring in.
Digital marketing firm Sensor Tower estimates that GTA 6 generated $2.36 billion in pre-orders and first-day sales, with approximately 24.5 million copies sold following its Thursday release. GTA 6 costs $79.99 for PS5 and Xbox , with an "ultimate" version priced at $99.99. Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two have yet to confirm official sales figures but described demand as "unprecedented."
Players began pre-loading GTA 6 last week, even though they probably had to clear some space on their consoles. Millions of people are expected to take time off work and school to play GTA 6 . Xbox has a doctor's note from DJ Khaled (aka Dr. Xbox) that may be the excuse you need (but you'll probably want to clear it with your boss either way).
PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing.
Here's what people are saying about GTA VI . Just be warned: there are spoilers ahead for those who haven't played all the way through yet.
Now that the game has been out for more than 24 hours, players are starting to offer tips on how to navigate some of the early GTA 6 gameplay.
For instance, there's a whole checklist of things Jason should do before he leaves his safehouse. Some gamers advise that not every fight in GTA 6 has to end with a murder (which conveniently applies in the real world as well). There are suggestions on how to drive to a mission without wrecking every car, and advice on how to handle hostile NPCs .
There are tips out there for newbies to Vice City and Leonida, tricks to finding hidden loot and ideas for the best ways to evade the police.
On the topic of cheat codes, PC Gamer reports that GTA 6 handles them differently than in past GTA games: You have to complete all 91 GTA 6 story missions before you can access any cheat codes and find out what they do.
Grand Theft Auto diehards will be happy to see some of the characters from earlier games return in GTA 6 — but there's one familiar face that may not be welcomed with open arms.
It's confirmed that Jimmy De Santa makes a comeback in the new game, as a "crypto guy nepo baby" influencer. According to GTA Boom , Jimmy seems to know Jason, one of the GTA 6 main characters. He's voiced once again by actor Danny Tamberelli.
Jimmy has been a divisive character among GTA V fans, with some finding him more relatable than the game's more hardcore criminals and others comparing him (unfavorably) to AJ, the oafish son of crime boss Tony Soprano in HBO's hit show.
All good things come to an end, and in GTA 6 , players are starting to discover all the possible endings. Rockstar Games has confirmed there are "a lot more than two" ways the game can end. We won't spoil them here, but as is to be expected, people are already sharing the ones they've experienced online and chatting with other players about them.
While there's no official "good" or "bad" ending, how Jason and Lucia wind up depends entirely on the choices players make along the way. Their relationship status, the amount of money they have left and their criminal behavior all contribute to how they fare at the conclusion of the final mission.
Regardless of how the gameplay winds up, after the end credits, players are transported back to before the final mission. They can then keep exploring Leonida and Vice City, and work on any uncompleted side quests if they wish.
As is to be expected with such a massive game, players have begun to discover glitches in GTA 6. One that's received a lot of attention is a glitch that lets you override the game's third-person POV to play in first person. GTA 6 launched with only third-person mode available, but the ability to play in first person might be accessible in the game.
If you want to try out this glitch, go into your controller settings and change the Touch Pad Button setting from Map to Camera. Get in the driver's seat of your car in GTA 6 and press the up arrow on your controller's D pad, which lets the character pull out his phone. Put the phone away by pressing the circle or B button on your controller, then spam (repeatedly click) the touch pad button a few times. After this, the first-person glitch should kick in.
To return to third-person view, you'll have to reload your save.
Whether Rockstar Games will officially enable first-person mode in the game eventually, or fix this glitch, isn't clear yet.
The protagonist of Grand Theft Auto IV , Niko Bellic and his story arc were GTA fan favorites. He was briefly referenced in GTA V, but many wondered if we'd see him in GTA VI.
It's not until late in the game, but a gray-haired, weathered Bellic is included in Chapter 5 of GTA VI , as The Hitman in the "Taking Liberties" mission. No word yet if he ever gets to go bowling with his cousin, but it's confirmed that Bellic interacts with GTA VI main characters Jason and Lucia.
According to the official Rockstar Games GTA VI credits , the character is once again voiced by actor Michael Hollick
The physical copy of GTA 6 does not include a disc.
GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen says the video game industry's shift away from physical discs has hurt consumers — an issue highlighted by the launch of GTA 6 .
The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies.
"When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen told Bloomberg . "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop."
Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.
Asked about GTA 6 presales, Cohen said, "It's a code in a box. I mean, we're selling a lot of it."
Cohen declined to name specific companies. Take-Two Interactive, the company behind GTA 6 , declined to comment to Bloomberg.
Jason and Lucia in GTA 6 .
Romance is optional in GTA VI .
Rockstar has confirmed that players can decide whether the protagonists, Jason and Lucia, pursue a romantic relationship or keep things strictly platonic.
In an interview with Game Informer , Rockstar's Luke Howard explained that while the pair will always share a close working relationship, players will have the final say over whether their bond develops into something more.
The choice will also affect how certain scenes unfold. Rockstar has recorded alternate dialogue and performances to reflect the relationship players choose to pursue.
And it seems plenty of fans are hoping love wins out.
"Overall, we've seen that players are invested in supporting Jason and Lucia's relationship, but we don't favor a specific path through the game. It is completely down to player choice," Rockstar's Katie Pica said.
One U.S. Army unit offered a perk for soldiers who reenlisted: four days off to play GTA 6.
At Fort Stewart in Georgia, 43 soldiers agreed to extend their service by two to six years partly in exchange for a long weekend timed to coincide with the game's release.
The offer was open to 130 eligible soldiers in the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion from Aug. 1 to Nov. 14, according to ABC News .
The four-day pass came on top of standard reenlistment benefits, including potential cash bonuses and career opportunities. One soldier received more than $60,000 in bonuses along with the extra time off.

articles.title_orig: European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
articles.title_zh: European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of European troops are taking part in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends .
Meanwhile, as the drill was underway, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian missile had crashed early on Friday near Poland’s border with Ukraine, describing it as likely an intentional provocation by Moscow that was timed to the drills.
The crash site of the missile is about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the exercises.
“This was not an accidental event. It was coordinated with our show of force, our show of unity,” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Friday during a news conference at the drills.
“Our presence here shows that we cannot be frightened.”
Led by France and the United Kingdom, the multinational force is a non-NATO military initiative of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a wider political group of 37 nations supporting Ukraine.
The two-week exercise, which began on Nov. 9, is for the first time checking this coalition’s ability to deploy in Ukraine once the war ends.
It is aimed both at testing deployment plans and sending a message to Russia and the Trump administration that European countries are stepping up militarily.
Leaders from Ukraine and nearly 40 other delegations met in Berlin on Thursday to underline their support for Kyiv and explore Ukraine’s postwar security arrangements.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again. Moscow wants to keep NATO away from its borders.
US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine.
He and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure European leaders about US President Trump’s discussions on ending the nearly five-year-old war at his historic trilateral talks Thursday with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China.
Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, according to Kushner.
Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance’s Article 5, in which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
After Thursday’s meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the drill in Poland shows that the “Coalition of the Willing is ready to contribute with the United States of America to securing a peace.”
Around 2,800 personnel from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and the UK are taking part in the exercise, with Poland providing the logistical backup. Turkey was participating remotely from Istanbul.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that 1,100 troops from France were deployed, and that “we have terrestrial, air but also maritime operations, a dozen countries that are active in this coalition.”
The exercise in Poland follows 12 months of planning by the Multinational Force-Ukraine, or MNF-U, said UK brigadier Campbell Close, who serves as deputy commander for operations of the French Army’s 1st division. That division is in charge of the land part of the “Koalicja” exercise in Poland.
“This is a deployment exercise,” Close said on Monday at the Nowa Dęba military training ground in southeastern Poland. “We are a defensive force.”
He praised Poland’s handling of the logistics of moving thousands of vehicles, people and their equipment for the drill.
If deployed once a cease-fire is in place, the force would help regenerate Ukraine’s armed forces, provide the reassurance needed to open the country’s skies and help clear mines in the Black Sea, Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman, commander of MNF-U, has said. It would not have peacekeeping or peace-monitoring functions.
Coalition troops arrived in Poland by sea, air and land, the Polish government said, before traveling by rail and road to the Nowa Dęba training site.
They rehearsed transporting personnel and equipment, as well as joint command-and-control exercises, and flew fighter jets and an aerial refueling tanker.
They also operated surveillance drones, drilled responses to drone attacks and trained in trench warfare.
The initial idea of the Coalition of the Willing was to provide Ukraine with security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5.
In the absence of a NATO commitment to fulfill this function, France and the UK decided to go ahead with plans for a separate European proposal of countries willing to come to Ukraine’s aid if necessary.
Last year, Putin said that any foreign troops inside Ukraine would be considered “legitimate targets.”
The multinational troops may have a purely defensive function, but they would still need to be a “combat force for their own force protection,” said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow at the RUSI military think tank in London.

Two Danish men are suspected ​of having been recruited by Russian intelligence to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper ahead of a planned performance in Denmark , Danish ⁠broadcaster DR reported on Friday, citing a court hearing.
Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested the two men shortly before the rapper ⁠Kyivstoner's September 25 concert, which ​was ⁠later cancelled.
Both men denied any wrongdoing in court, DR reported.
The Russian ⁠embassy in Copenhagen did not immediately reply to ​a ⁠request for comment.
Denmark's national ‌security and intelligence service, PET, Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen and Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen ‌were due to hold press ‌briefings later on Friday to address the suspected assassination plan.
PET said in September Russia was recruiting ⁠Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defence firms with ties to Ukraine .
It was unclear how police identified the two men, who were stopped in a vehicle carrying several weapons, or how the investigation expanded to include ‌two other men who are not accused ​of participating in the alleged assassination ‌plot targeting Kyivstoner.
However, all ⁠four men have been held in ⁠custody since September, according to the broadcaster.
It was also ‌unclear how ​the Russian intelligence services allegedly ‌recruited the two Danish ​suspects.
Meanwhile, the number of children ​killed and injured in the Ukraine war so far this year has already surpassed last year's and is on track to rival the ⁠deadly first year of the conflict in 2022, the UN children's agency said on Friday.
Russian attacks on Ukraine have been intensifying this year, with long-range weapons being ⁠the chief cause of ​civilian deaths, ⁠according to the United Nations . Russia has repeatedly denied intentionally attacking civilian targets in ⁠Ukraine.
At least 1,144 children have been killed or ​injured ⁠in Ukraine in the ‌first ten months of 2026, UNICEF said, just below the 1,386 recorded in 2022, when Russia ‌invaded.
UNICEF's Louise Wateridge said that 114 ‌children had been killed and 1,030 injured through end-October and that the UN had verified around 270 attacks on ⁠education facilities this year. One was a Kyiv kindergarten in the Solomianskyi district that was hit for the second time on November 7, although there were no deaths or injuries since it was overnight.
"The children who came here should be learning ‌their colours. They should be learning their numbers ​and their first words," said Wateridge, speaking ‌from amid the playground wreckage ⁠in a televised briefing to journalists in ⁠Geneva.
"Instead, children across Ukraine are learning to recognize the sound ‌of the ​incoming drones. They're learning ‌to run for shelter," she ​said on World Children's Day.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock drops after first day of trading
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock drops after first day of trading
articles.content_orig:
A bruising stock market sell-off appeared to be gathering steam Friday morning, despite high hopes that Anthropic’s record-setting IPO a day earlier would revive sentiment around the flagging AI trade.
Instead, Friday’s early downturn was led by Anthropic itself, whose shares were down 10% after rising 17% on its first day on the Nasdaq Composite.
The S&P 500 was trading 1% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs.
Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 2%. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also fell in the premarket.
The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index’s longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn.
Given the importance the AI trade has played this year in propelling markets and economic growth writ large, its derailment amid concerns about costs, debt, profitability and political risk could have broader implications.
Investor concerns about AI revenues tied to exports of advanced technology to China compounded the sell-off.
The Jensen Huang scandal pulling down Nvidia appeared to broaden Thursday, when a short-selling firm issued a report raising questions about whether Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, may also have had shipments to Asia diverted to mainland China.
Alongside the stock sell-off, there has been an increase in purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeing signs of weakening growth amid higher interest rates from the Federal Reserve and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.
Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Modera Wealth Management, called the recent sell-off “a garden-variety correction.”
But he noted that overall returns have still been respectable this year, “especially against a challenging backdrop of rising rates, persistent inflation and fears about an AI slowdown.”
But a prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth.
“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang wasn't mentioned in latest talks with China, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang wasn't mentioned in latest talks with China, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not mentioned in the Trump administration's latest talks with China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Friday.
"No," Bessent said without elaborating when asked if Huang, a close ally of President Donald Trump facing allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy, had come up in those talks.
Bessent also suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the discussions.
"We've already agreed that the that H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.
Bessent's appearance came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other countries' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
There was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI, Bessent told CNBC.
They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.
In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Secretary Howard Lutnick , for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cut-outs like Megaspeed, the Singaporean company at the center of Huang's spy-sex scandal.
Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight lipped.
Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."
"I think we are going to see that the the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.

articles.title_orig: WATCH LIVE: Trump holds news conference after China trip
articles.title_zh: WATCH LIVE: Trump holds news conference after China trip
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.title_zh: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.content_orig:
Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough."
He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.
Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."
Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."
His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.
Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.
"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.
The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.
Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.
Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.
A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.
GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.
That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."
When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.
Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.
Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.
"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."
Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.
Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.
"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

articles.title_orig: Did Banks Get Hacked? Visa, Mastercard, Chase Confirm Vendor Cyberattack
articles.title_zh: Did Banks Get Hacked? Visa, Mastercard, Chase Confirm Vendor Cyberattack
articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Watch: Trump to hold press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
articles.title_zh: Watch: Trump to hold press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
articles.content_orig:
In a pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and President Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
President Trump is set to hold a White House press conference today at noon, following his return to Washington after a four-day trip to Asia , where he sat down for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.
Watch the 12 p.m. ET news conference live:
The U.S. president said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.
Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.
While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.
"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."
Foreign trips are often largely about the pomp and circumstance involved in meetings between heads of state. Among other special events, Trump's arrival in China, for example, included a military flyover and young dancers.
But the events are also extensively choreographed, with aides working months in advance to lock down agreements and commitments that the leaders can point to as evidence of a successful trip. That did not appear to be a main objective for this visit.
For Xi, he was able to boast of China's global leadership by bringing together the world's greatest nuclear powers to discuss global challenges.
For Putin, the meeting allowed a chance to reestablish Russia as a great geopolitical power on par with China and the U.S.
And for Trump, it's a chance to turn the page and demonstrate his ongoing power at a time when he's been weakened domestically after the devastating midterm elections.
In his opening remarks alongside Xi and Putin, Trump said the three leaders were making history and that they had a responsibility to the rest of the world to maintain open and respectful dialogue.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite," Trump said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech."
But while the kind words and pats on the back were prevalent, the lack of deliverables was also noteworthy.
It has raised questions about Trump's approach to foreign policy.
Trump has spent much of the last few years trying to replace the postwar rules-based order, ripping up traditional alliances in favor of a more personal approach to diplomacy. He prefers to work out deals personally with the world's superpowers.
But the visit may be demonstrating that access does not always produce results.
Xi and Putin have their own strategic objectives, which are not going to change because they're friendly with Trump. As Maloney put it, they also have to calculate whether agreements reached with Trump can survive domestic scrutiny or a change of administration in the coming years.
"I think both Putin and Xi recognized that President Trump's time is beginning to wane," Maloney said, "that his command of U.S. politics is also beginning to wane, and they're going to be looking to who and what may be coming next."

articles.title_orig: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.title_zh: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck a deal on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian Drones Hit Key Russian Oil Hub 1,300 Kilometers From Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian Drones Hit Key Russian Oil Hub 1,300 Kilometers From Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Kaleykino oil pumping station in Tatarstan, a major hub in Russia's pipeline network, damaging oil storage tanks. Separate drone attacks were reported in Kursk, where buildings and vehicles were damaged.
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Kaleykino oil pumping station in Russia ‘s Republic of Tatarstan early on Thursday, Nov. 19, targeting a key hub in the country’s trunk oil pipeline network located around 1,300 kilometers (808 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The independent Russian news outlet Astra reported that the facility, located 5-8 kilometers (3-5 miles) from the city of Almetyevsk, was targeted in the attack. Local residents reportedly saw ambulances and fire trucks heading toward the station afterward.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Astra later reported that Tatarstan authorities had confirmed a Ukrainian drone attack on oil storage tanks near Almetyevsk, while also acknowledging damage to civilian infrastructure.
“Early this morning, enemy drones attacked the southeastern part of the republic. Oil storage tanks near Almetyevsk were struck,” a statement from the press office of Tatarstan Rais Rustam Minnikhanov said.
Regional authorities added debris had damaged several civilian structures but reported no deaths or injuries.
“An automatic fire-extinguishing system and the well-coordinated efforts of the facility’s security services helped to quickly contain the blaze, preventing a major fire,” the statement said.
Emergency response teams and equipment were deployed at the site, the Kazan Kremlin press service added.
Later, Ukraine’s General Staff has confirmed a strike on the Kaleykino-1 oil pumping station in Russia, reporting that three massive oil storage tanks were hit in an attack carried out on Thursday.
In a report released on Friday, Nov. 20, the General Staff said one of the tanks caught fire, while the other two sustained damage.
“It has been confirmed that three RVSPA-50000 storage tanks at the Kaleykino-1 oil pumping station were hit; these are among the largest oil storage tanks built in Russia. One of them caught fire, while the other two sustained damage,” the report said.
According to the General Staff, the strike affects more than an isolated oil facility, disrupting a key link in Russia’s oil supply chain.
The scale of the damage is underscored by the size and complexity of the storage tanks hit in the attack, as per the report.
Each RVSPA-50000 tank is a steel structure approximately 60 meters in diameter and as tall as a six-story building, with a storage capacity of up to 50,000 cubic meters of oil.
The tanks are equipped with floating pontoons that rest on the surface of the oil to reduce evaporation. Constructing a single tank requires hundreds of tons of steel and takes months.
According to the General Staff’s description, construction involves preparing a specialized foundation, welding the tank walls together ring by ring, and then carrying out rigorous testing with water.
Such structures cannot be replaced or restored overnight, the General Staff added.
The Kaleykino pumping station is a critical part of Russia’s oil transportation infrastructure and is owned by state-controlled pipeline operator Transneft.
The facility serves as a major blending hub for different grades of crude oil arriving from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, Udmurtia and Bashkortostan. It also helps maintain pressure across the pipeline system and manages crude distribution, including supplies entering the Druzhba pipeline.
This was not the first reported Ukrainian drone attack on the facility. On Feb. 23, long-range Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the oil pumping station.
A source from Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry told Astra at the time that two storage tanks, each with a capacity of 50,000 cubic meters (about 13.2 million gallons), caught fire.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks were also reported in the Russian city of Kursk, where a fire broke out near the Kursk Music College-Boarding School for the Blind, according to Astra.
The outlet’s OSINT analysis of eyewitness footage identified the area around building No. 23A on Karl Marx Street as the location of the fire. The site houses the music college and boarding school, its dormitory at 23/1 Karl Marx Street, and nearby private residences.
“Black smoke is rising from behind building No. 23A on Karl Marx Street in Kursk following a drone attack,” Astra reported.
Eyewitnesses described several strikes and damage to nearby buildings.
The Telegram channel Pepel.Kursk also reported that vehicles were on fire in central Kursk following a drone explosion and that one person had been injured, although it did not specify the exact location.
Earlier, Kursk region Governor Alexander Khinshtein said Russian air defenses had been activated over the city and that smoke had been reported coming from a building in the center. He said details were being verified.
In a separate update covering the previous 24 hours, Khinshtein reported that debris from downed drones had partially damaged six apartment buildings and one private residence in Kursk. No fatalities were reported.
The governor also said a 57-year-old man had been injured after stepping on an explosive device while loading beets in the village of Sopelovka in Kurchatovsky District. He was taken to Kursk Regional Hospital for treatment.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 53 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Nov. 18 and 8 a.m. on Nov. 19.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk and Tula regions, as well as the Republic of Tatarstan.
Since the beginning of November, Ukrainian drones have also attacked the Samara linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) twice.
Following one of the strikes, a fire at the facility burned for several days before being extinguished.
The Samara station is one of Russia’s largest oil transportation and distribution hubs, connecting four major pipelines: Almetyevsk-Kuybyshev, Kaltasinsky-Kuybyshev, Nizhnevartovsk-Kurgan-Kuybyshev and Guryev-Kuybyshev.
It receives oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region and Kazakhstan before distributing it through the pipeline network.
Separately, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Territory overnight on Nov. 18. The two facilities, among the largest in southern Russia, were targeted for the second time this November.
Ukraine’s General Staff said explosions and smoke were reported near the Ilsky refinery, where storage tanks were hit. At the Afipsky facility, an oil processing unit was reportedly struck.
Additionally, on Nov. 20, the General Staff clarified that strike on the Ilsky refinery destroyed one RVS-5000 storage tank and damaged eight others: seven RVS-5000 tanks and one RVS-1000 tank.
A section of an oil pipeline, five technical buildings, and a warehouse were also damaged. The full extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The two refineries have a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 13 million tons (95 million barrels) of crude oil and supply fuel to Russian forces in the south.
General Staff added the refinery strikes were part of its efforts to disrupt Russian military logistics and revenue from oil exports.
Ukraine resumed its campaign against Russian oil refineries in late October, striking around 10 of Russia’s 35 facilities in recent weeks. The attacks have contributed to a roughly 30% drop in daily crude processing, from about 700,000 tons (5.1 million barrels per day) at the end of October to 500,000 tons (3.7 million barrels per day) by mid-November, according to sources cited by Reuters.
The decline has also contributed to gasoline shortages and sales restrictions in at least eight Russian regions. In Moscow, Rosneft gas

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Sells $32 Billion of AI Chip Debt at Yields Topping 8%
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Sells $32 Billion of AI Chip Debt at Yields Topping 8%
articles.content_orig:
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel .
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Debt-funded AI ambitions are now testing SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction ), which has slipped below its IPO price. SpaceX stock is at $131.16, down 5% in morning trading. That drop adds to an 11% decline over the past month.
Two reports on the financing behind SpaceX founder Elon Musk’s AI chip plans are fueling the selling. The broader AI sell-off continues as well, with the NASDAQ 100 down 1% and technology the weakest sector. Growth in the AI business underpins the company’s valuation, since SpaceX’s AI Solutions & Infrastructure segment revenue reached $7.60 billion [ 1 ] in Q3 2026, up 830% year over year (YoY).
The Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that lenders backing SpaceX’s debt package tried to restrict Musk from launching the NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) chips securing the financing into space. Lenders feared they couldn’t recover and sell the chips if SpaceX defaulted. It’s unclear whether those restrictions made it into the final agreement.
Bloomberg reported that SpaceX raised $32 billion [ 2 ] in bonds to buy AI chips as part of a $40 billion financing package that includes bank loans. That money funds a five-year lease of NVIDIA processors. Goldman Sachs ( NYSE:GS ) arranged the three-part deal with Apollo Global Management, and Pacific Investment Management Company (PIMCO) was among several large funds that bought into the SpaceX debt.
The largest tranche of SpaceX’s chip-backed notes paid a yield well above the average for U.S. investment-grade corporate bonds, according to Bloomberg. In plain terms, bond buyers charged SpaceX extra because of the deal’s unusual structure and the risks tied to AI infrastructure. Wall Street worries about debt-funded AI spending have been growing, including a warning from a major U.S. bank last week that heavy tech borrowing was straining demand for corporate bonds.
Rocket Lab ( NASDAQ:RKLB ) stock is at $49.67, down 3%. That decline is smaller than SpaceX’s. On November 9 [ 3 ] , the company reported record Q3 revenue of $267.83 million, up 72.7% YoY, alongside a record $3.57 billion backlog.
AST SpaceMobile ( NASDAQ:ASTS ) stock is at $25.18, down 1%. Measured against SpaceX and Rocket Lab, the AST SpaceMobile decline is the mildest of the three. Over a longer stretch, the stock is down 65% year to date (YTD). Management reaffirmed the company’s full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $150 million to $200 million [ 4 ] on November 9.
SpaceX runs a vertically integrated business that pairs Falcon and Starship launches with Starlink connectivity and a fast-growing AI arm built around Grok, Cursor and its COLOSSUS II compute buildout. That AI arm is what the chip-backed debt supports, which ties SpaceX more closely to the AI infrastructure trade (we profiled seven suppliers powering that buildout, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here ) than any pure space company.
Rocket Lab is an end-to-end space company built on launch services through Electron and the upcoming Neutron, plus spacecraft and components for government and commercial customers. AST SpaceMobile builds BlueBird satellites that connect directly to standard smartphones and works through mobile network operators to reach customers. Each company has heavy capital needs of its own, but SpaceX’s debt questions center on AI hardware.
The bulls see a chance to own SpaceX below its offer price while its AI business grows rapidly and the company’s compute financing is now in place. Large bond funds still committed money to the deal, which suggests deep-pocketed institutions remain willing to back SpaceX’s plans.
On the other side, the bears argue that a yield premium that steep points to rising risk, especially if lenders worry about recovering collateral that could end up in orbit. Growing unease over debt-funded AI spending could keep SpaceX stock under pressure while the AI trade stays shaky.
SpaceX’s next test is whether the stock can reclaim its IPO price as more details of the chip financing terms emerge. Investors may want to track how the debate over SpaceX’s chip-backed debt resolves before drawing any firm conclusions.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock extends 6-day losing streak, as AMD, Broadcom lead chip sector lower
articles.content_orig:
By Sean Williams – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:06AM EST
10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›
On Oct. 6, Nvidia ( NVDA -6.85% ) peaked at an intraday high of $243.37 per share, reaching a valuation of $5.78 trillion. The face of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out holds a virtual monopoly in enterprise data centers with its several generations of graphics processing units (GPUs).
But it's been a bumpy ride over the last six weeks. Between its Oct. 6 intraday peak and the Nov. 17 close, Nvidia lost $2.03 trillion in valuation. In just six weeks, Nvidia lost more in market value than all but five S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.69% ) companies... one of which is itself .
Image source: Getty Images.
While Nvidia's historically inexpensive valuation and its jaw-dropping Data Center segment growth suggest its stock is a bargain, it's also possible that its recent downtrend is just beginning .
Let's not beat around the bush: the resignation of now-former CEO Jensen Huang following an admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and allegations of extramarital relations with up to two employees has left Nvidia without an identity.
Although Nvidia has an extensive order backlog, superior GPUs, and its pricing power continues to be aided by GPU supply shortages, the company's innovation schedule (bringing an advanced AI chip to market annually) and its circular financing deals are very much in question.
BREAKING: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has opened an investigation into Nvidia, $NVDA, amid the Jensen Huang situation, per WSJ.

The focus of the investigation includes whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.

The Justice Department is also now reportedly leading multiple investigations involving Alice Huang.
Furthermore, Huang's actions and departure may have breached the trust of clients, consumers, and/or investors. Earlier this week, the Securities and Exchange Commission opened an investigation over whether the company misled investors in its disclosures.
Without trust, Nvidia becomes practically uninvestable .
Although long-term trends strongly suggest that AI will be a game changer and that the benchmark S&P 500 will head higher, historical precedent isn't Nvidia's friend over the short run .
Every next-big-thing technology since (and including) the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s has navigated an early-innings bubble. These bubbles form because investors consistently overestimate the pace of adoption and optimization of hyped innovations.
NASDAQ · As of 11:41 AM ET 11/20/26
The good news for AI is that there isn't an adoption issue. Nvidia's quarterly results make it clear that businesses are freely spending to build out their data centers.
But it's an entirely different story when it comes to optimizing this technology. It took until well after the dot-com bubble burst before businesses figured out how to optimize internet-driven solutions to maximize sales and profits. As with the internet, AI will take time to mature , leaving Nvidia and its peers exposed to a possible bubble-bursting event.
Image source: Getty Images.
Lastly, Nvidia's fiscal fourth-quarter gross margin is forecast to dip to 71%-72% from a reported 74.8% (based on generally accepted accounting principles, or GAAP ) in the fiscal third quarter.
Although Nvidia's GAAP gross margin has pretty consistently hovered in the low-to-mid 70% range over the trailing three years, the company's fiscal fourth-quarter forecast must have some investors wondering if this is as good as it gets.
NVDA Gross Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts.
This two- to three-percentage-point dip in GAAP gross margin reflects higher memory prices and the near-term ramp-up associated with Vera Rubin shipments. But if GPU supply picks up from its competition, as is expected, Nvidia's pricing power and GAAP gross margin would be expected to wane over time.
In other words, Nvidia may not be the slam-dunk bargain it appears to be.

articles.title_orig: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.title_zh: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.content_orig:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.
Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period , using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.
The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.
Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.
During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.
The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.
The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.
In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.
"This is simply unacceptable."
Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.
"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.
"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."
Kate Parker, criminal barrister and founder of the Schools Consent Project, said legally, a third party or a partner cannot consent on a person's behalf.
"The law makes that very clear. A person consents if he or she agrees by choice and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice," she added.
"In a case like this where someone has been made unconscious, there is no possible way that that person is able to consent because of course they have no capacity."
She added that the defendants' claims that they thought Joanne Young had consented through her husband "doesn't make sense legally, and that's not a legal position that can be supported in court".
Parker said the defence used by the four men in the trial is not a correct application of the law but might be something defence lawyers would try and rely on as their client's genuine belief in their victim's consent, or in mitigation to try and get a lower sentence.
Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.
"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.
"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."
Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.
"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.
"So why are they still accessible?" she said.
Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.
"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.
"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."
Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.
"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.
"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help others when this has happened to them."
Zoe Watts is the founder of a global campaign called End Eye Check that works to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse.
Like Joanne Young and Bishop, Watts waived her right to anonymity after she was drugged and raped by her husband.
Watts hopes that Joanne Young's case "sets a precedent", but told Woman's Hour that the crime is more widespread than many realise.
"I have had women contact me from 25 different countries," she said.
"It's a daily process of women either contacting me because they've woken up to find their husband having sex with them while they're asleep and have done on numerous occasions.
"Or perhaps they're not sure if they've been drugged or maybe they are genuinely asleep and wake up and find him that way, or women that have found videos or recordings on their phone of things they haven't consented to," Watts added.
Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC that more needs to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.
"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.
"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.
"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."
Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told Radio 4's Woman's Hour that current laws do not do enough to protect women.
"The law says that somebody can seek a defence to defend themselves against a rape claim if they reasonably believe that they had consent," said Phillips.
"These people went on to argue that they reasonably believed that Joanne's husband had sought her consent and got it.
"They were found guilty, but it's whether the law needs to explicitly say, 'you cannot reasonably believe someone's given consent unless they have given it'.
"If there was clarity in the law, Joanne wouldn't have been put through the court case," Phillips added.
She also believes that more needs to be done to hold the websites hosting adverts and similar content to account.
"Can every pornographic site in our country categorically say that not one of these snuff videos or sedated videos is on their site?
"Unless they can guarantee it with a signed piece of paper from the person that they know is in that video [they should not be published]," Phillips said.

articles.title_orig: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.title_zh: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was visiting Poland on Friday, said: "The impact of Russia's illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday's incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Even as Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders gathered for high-profile photos at the summit's close, key issues from Nvidia to Taiwan remained unaddressed.
"The intrigue is around not what was said, but what remains unresolved," said Gary Dvorchak, managing director at Blueshirt.
"Taiwan remains a major source of strategic uncertainty. North Korea was notably absent from the trilateral nuclear declaration," he said. "Southeast Asia, which is increasingly central to global manufacturing and investment, was overshadowed by major-power diplomacy."
President Donald Trump did not meet with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, despite speculation .
Taiwan, one of the 21 member economies of APEC, sent Acer Group founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih to Shenzhen. But the self-governed island, which Beijing claims is part of its territory, did not feature in any significant way during the event. Taiwan is set to hold key elections for Taipei mayor and other posts on Nov. 28.
Instead, the highlight of this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen was a trilateral meeting Thursday between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin . The three leaders, meeting together for the first time, reaffirmed interests in reducing nuclear risks and plans to increase oil production.
"The optics are impressive, but there's not much happening," Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, said Friday of the trilateral on CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ."
Resolving the years-long Ukraine war would require involvement from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies, Bremmer said.
Ahead of the trilateral, Trump and Xi also held their third bilateral summit of the year. Xi greeted Trump at the airport late Wednesday, reciprocating the hospitality shown in September when the Chinese leader visited Washington.
But little was shared publicly on whether the two countries agreed to reduce tariffs further, allow rare earths to keep flowing beyond a January deadline, or address tech competition.
Recent reports tying Jensen Huang to an alleged Chinese spy led to the executive's resignation as Nvidia CEO. It also raised questions in Congress about the effectiveness of U.S. efforts to restrict China's access to advanced chips used to train artificial intelligence.
Trump indicated to Fox News that Nvidia came up briefly in his talks with Xi. U.S. officials last week said Trump did not plan to raise the matter, while noting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would accompany the U.S. president.
No other executive was named. Other American business leaders, including Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, who also chairs the U.S.-China Business Council, joined the APEC CEO Summit and was seen at a welcome banquet Wednesday evening .
However, Musk did not appear with Trump at major APEC-related events. CNBC was present for the opening portions of a banquet Wednesday and the Economic Leaders' Meeting Thursday and did not see Musk.
In fact, Musk flew to Shanghai Thursday morning to visit Tesla's factory there, a company executive said on Chinese social media . Musk also showed up in a social media video with Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.
Musk addressed Wednesday's DealBook Summit in New York via video conference, having previously said on X that he would be joining from China.
Tesla and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
"We still don't have a durable resolution of the U.S.-China trade dispute," Dvorchak said, adding: "Business needs certainty, not just ceremony."
Trump visited Shenzhen after briefly traveling to the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping happening on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. Trump also met the prime minister of Thailand, Anutin Charnvirakul.
Topics of discussion included U.S. cooperation with the region, trade and critical minerals, U.S. Ambassador to ASEAN Kevin Kim told reporters Wednesday. He declined to comment on whether China's influence in the region was addressed.
Kim emphasized it was the second year in a row that Trump visited Southeast Asia, and noted the region "will be at the heart of SI [artificial intelligence] going forward," making it important that American technology is "getting into the right hands" through a regulatory framework the president is building.
Speaking to reporters a day later in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also highlighted the ASEAN and Quad events over APEC. "The major outcome of this diplomatic week was the Quad Summit," she said, noting via official English translation how the four leaders expressed " strong opposition to the unilateral approach to change the status quo by force or coercion ... [as well as] arbitrary export control."
Takaichi, the first Japanese leader in seven years to visit China, received a cool reception upon her arrival in Shenzhen for the APEC meeting.
Tensions between Japan and China have escalated since Takaichi drew Beijing's ire in Nov. 2025 when she said that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could draw a Japanese military response.
Takaichi said Thursday that Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communiqué.
The communique said Japan "understands and respects" the People's Republic of China's position on Taiwan, but does not explicitly acknowledge Taiwan as part of the PRC.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
articles.title_zh: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering , bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday.
The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX , which held a record IPO in June.
Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."
Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in premarket trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.
In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices , Google , Microsoft , Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.
Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout .
CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI , now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.
The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic.
"For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'"
